title: Infratentorial benign cystic meningioma mimicking a hemangioblastoma radiologically and a pilocytic astrocytoma intraoperatively: a case report
case_prompt:
A 30-year-old Chinese woman with a remote history of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia in remission presented with a 3-week history of worsening headaches, giddiness, and vomiting. Neurological examination revealed cerebellar signs consistent with an infratentorial mass. Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the head showed a large (4.0 × 4.1 × 4.8 cm) posterior fossa cystic mass with an eccentrically located enhancing nodule measuring 1.5 × 1.9 cm. The lesion compressed the midbrain and fourth ventricle, resulting in dilation of the third and lateral ventricles and tonsillar herniation. 

Subsequent MRI confirmed the cystic posterior fossa mass with an eccentrically located nodule adjacent to the vein of Galen. The nodule was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, hypointense on T1-weighted images, and showed avid gadolinium enhancement. No dural-tail enhancement was seen. Periventricular FLAIR hyperintensities were consistent with acute hydrocephalus. MR spectroscopy of the nodule demonstrated a reversal of the choline-to-creatine ratio with slight reduction in the N-acetylaspartate peak. Diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC mapping showed restricted diffusion within the mural nodule. After review, a radiological diagnosis of hemangioblastoma was made, and the patient was scheduled for surgical resection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hemangioblastoma was considered given the lesion’s characteristic cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellar region but was argued against by the absence of a high mobile lipid peak on MRS — “It has been reported that the presence of high mobile lipid on proton MRS is more suggestive of hemangioblastoma, which was not seen in this case.”  
2. Pilocytic astrocytoma was included in the initial differential because of the tumor’s cystic appearance with a mural nodule in a young adult — “The initial radiological differential diagnosis of hemangioblastoma or pilocytic astrocytoma was based on the tumor’s characteristic appearance and location.”  
3. Astrocytoma was considered as one of the intracranial cystic masses that can mimic cystic meningiomas — “They can suggest other intracranial cystic masses: hemangioblastoma, astrocytoma, neuroblastoma or a metastatic tumor with a cystic or necrotic component.”  
4. Neuroblastoma was listed among other cystic intracranial lesions that could appear similar on imaging — “They can suggest other intracranial cystic masses: hemangioblastoma, astrocytoma, neuroblastoma or a metastatic tumor with a cystic or necrotic component.”  
5. Metastatic tumor was part of the radiological differential for cystic or necrotic intracranial masses — “They can suggest other intracranial cystic masses: hemangioblastoma, astrocytoma, neuroblastoma or a metastatic tumor with a cystic or necrotic component.”  
6. Partly enhanced glioma was considered because MRI cannot reliably distinguish cystic meningiomas from cystic gliomas due to non-enhanced cysts and focal edema — “cystic meningiomas may not be differentiated from partly enhanced glioma or metastasis on MRI because of their non-enhanced cyst and focal oedema.”  
7. Anaplastic meningioma was noted as another high-grade lesion with similar MRS lipid peaks, although specificity is poor — “the lipid peak on the MRS is non-specific and is also observed in other high-grade tumors such as high-grade gliomas, metastatic tumor, and anaplastic meningioma.”
